title: IP vs BP vs USP vs EP Grade: What's the Difference and Which Should You Use?
metaTitle: IP vs BP vs USP vs EP Grade Explained | Surravi Phharma
metaDescription: What is the difference between IP, BP, USP, and EP grades in pharmaceuticals? Learn which grade your formulation needs and why it matters for...
excerpt: One of the most common questions from pharmaceutical formulators in India is: which pharmacopoeial grade should I specify — IP, BP, USP, or EP? The answer depends on where your product is registered, who your end customer is, and what your formulation requires.

content.text: One of the most common questions we receive from pharmaceutical formulators, procurement managers, and nutraceutical brands is: which grade should I order — IP, BP, USP, or EP? The short answer is that all four are equivalent in terms of purity and quality, but each is published by a different national or regional pharmacopoeia. The right choice depends on where your product will be registered and sold..
What is a Pharmacopoeia?

A pharmacopoeia is an official compendium of standards for medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients, published by a government or regulatory authority. It defines the tests, procedures, and acceptance criteria that a pharmaceutical ingredient must meet to be considered of acceptable quality. Using pharmacopoeial-grade materials is a core requirement of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) worldwide.
IP — Indian Pharmacopoeia

The Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) is published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. For any pharmaceutical product registered and sold in India under Schedule M of the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, excipients and APIs listed in the IP must comply with IP standards. IP is the default required grade for domestic Indian pharmaceutical formulations. If your product is only for the Indian market, IP grade is sufficient and is usually the most economical option.
BP — British Pharmacopoeia

The British Pharmacopoeia (BP) is published by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). BP grade is required for pharmaceutical products registered in the UK, Commonwealth countries, and many African and Middle Eastern markets that follow British pharmaceutical standards. BP grade materials are also widely accepted in India for export formulations and by multinational pharmaceutical companies operating manufacturing facilities in India.
EP — European Pharmacopoeia

The European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur. or EP) is published by the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines (EDQM) and is the mandatory standard for pharmaceutical products registered in all 37 European Pharmacopoeia member states. EP grade is required for products exported to the European Union. Importantly, the BP monographs for most excipients are aligned with EP monographs — so a material meeting BP generally meets EP as well.
USP — United States Pharmacopeia

The USP-NF (United States Pharmacopeia – National Formulary) is published by the United States Pharmacopoeial Convention and is required for pharmaceutical products registered with the US FDA. USP grade is mandatory for any product exported to the United States or manufactured to FDA-approved specifications. USP is also widely adopted globally by innovator pharmaceutical companies as their voluntary internal quality standard. For parenteral (injectable) formulations and high-purity applications, USP grade often has the most stringent endotoxin and particulate matter requirements.
Are IP, BP, EP, and USP grades chemically the same?

For most common pharmaceutical excipients and active ingredients, the quality of the material meeting any of these standards is functionally equivalent — all specify high purity, defined assay ranges, and strict limits on impurities, heavy metals, and microbiological contamination. The differences between pharmacopoeias are primarily in the specific test methods and acceptance criteria used to verify quality, not in the actual purity of the material itself.

However, there are cases where specifications differ meaningfully. Mannitol IP and USP both require 98.0–102.0% assay, but differ in specific test methodologies. Some newer EP monographs have stricter elemental impurity limits following ICH Q3D guidelines. Always review the specific monograph for your ingredient if regulatory precision matters.
Which grade should you specify for Indian pharmaceutical manufacturing?

For domestic Indian formulations — IP grade is sufficient and is the most cost-effective choice. For export to UK and Commonwealth markets — specify BP. For export to Europe — specify EP (or BP, which is harmonised with EP for most monographs). For export to the USA or FDA-regulated formulations — specify USP. For multi-market products — specify USP/BP/EP, as these are the most globally accepted standards. Many manufacturers in India specify multi-pharmacopoeial compliance (e.g., IP/BP/USP compliant) to maintain flexibility.

title: How to Read a Certificate of Analysis (COA) for Pharmaceutical Ingredients
metaTitle: How to Read a COA: Pharma Ingredient Guide | Surravi Phharma
metaDescription: Learn how to read a Certificate of Analysis (COA) for pharma excipients and APIs. Key sections, red flags to check, and what to verify before you accept a batch.
excerpt: Every batch of a pharmaceutical ingredient should arrive with a Certificate of Analysis, but many buyers only check that the document exists. Here is how to actually read a COA and spot problems before the material reaches your production floor.

content.text: When a shipment of excipients or active ingredients arrives at your facility, the Certificate of Analysis (COA) is the first document your quality team will ask for. Yet in our experience supplying manufacturers across India, many buyers only confirm that a COA is attached, without checking whether it actually proves the material is fit for use. This guide explains what a COA contains, how to read it, and what to check before you release a batch.
What is a Certificate of Analysis?

A Certificate of Analysis is a batch-specific quality document issued by the manufacturer's quality control laboratory. It lists the tests performed on a particular batch, the acceptance limits for each test, and the actual results obtained. It is not a general product brochure. A COA belongs to one batch, and it should be traceable to that batch through the batch or lot number printed on the container label.
Key sections of a COA

Header details: The top of the COA should show the product name, grade or pharmacopoeial standard (for example IP, BP, EP or USP), batch or lot number, manufacturing date, expiry or retest date, and the name and address of the manufacturer. If any of these are missing, ask for a corrected document.

Tests and specifications: This is a table listing each test, such as description, identification, assay, loss on drying, pH, heavy metals, residue on ignition and microbial limits. The specification column shows the acceptable range, and the result column shows what was measured for this batch.

Test method reference: A reliable COA states the method used for each test, usually by referring to the relevant pharmacopoeial monograph or an in-house validated method. This tells you what standard the results are measured against.
Approval and signature: The COA should be signed or authorised by a quality control or quality assurance representative, with a date. An unsigned or undated COA carries little weight during an audit.
How to check the results

Start by matching the batch number on the COA to the batch number on the drums, bags or cartons you received. Then compare every result against its specification. A result must fall within the stated limit, and the pharmacopoeia named on the COA must be the one you ordered. For example, if you ordered a USP grade material, a COA that references only an in-house specification is not sufficient.

Next, check the dates. Confirm that the manufacturing date and expiry or retest date are reasonable and leave you enough shelf life for your production plan. Finally, check that the assay and impurity results are reported as actual values rather than just the word Complies. Numerical results give your team something to trend from batch to batch.
Red flags to watch for

Be cautious if the COA has no batch number, if the batch number does not match the material, if all results sit exactly on the specification limit, or if the document looks edited or is a low-quality copy. Also watch for a COA that lists no test methods, no manufacturer details, or a pharmacopoeia edition that differs from what you specified. Any of these is a reason to pause and ask your supplier for clarification.
Manufacturer COA vs supplier COA

Distributors and importers often pass on the original manufacturer's COA. This is normal and is what most regulated buyers expect, because it traces the batch back to the site that made and tested it. Some buyers also carry out their own incoming quality control testing on top of the COA, which is good practice for critical materials. A COA reduces risk, but it does not replace your own sampling and verification procedures.
Documents that should accompany the COA

Depending on your product and regulatory needs, you may also request a Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS), a Technical Data Sheet (TDS), a GMP or manufacturing licence copy, and a declaration of origin. Asking for these at the time of supplier qualification saves time later, especially during customer or regulatory audits.
